# About this document {#sec-about .unnumbered}

On a cluster, you do not run a program; you ask for resources, and Slurm runs
your program when it can grant them. A job is a request: so many CPUs, so much
memory, and possibly GPUs, for so long. It waits in a queue until the resources
are free, and then its script runs inside them, and only inside them. Almost
everything that surprises newcomers follows from that: jobs that wait for
hours, jobs killed at their limits, and programs that run slower on the cluster
than on a laptop (@sec-model). Working with Slurm comes down to writing a job
script, submitting it, and finding out afterwards what the job used
(@sec-usage).

Every cluster configures Slurm its own way, with its own partitions, limits,
accounts, and file systems, which its documentation describes. This document
covers what holds on all of them. [](../containers/apptainer.qmd#sec-slurm)
shows how to run a container in a job, and workflow managers, such as Snakemake
and Nextflow, submit the jobs of their steps themselves.

Checked against Slurm 24.11.


# How Slurm thinks {#sec-model}

A cluster is many computers, the nodes, and one or a few login nodes in front
of them. Everyone logs in to the same login nodes, to edit, compile, move
files, and submit jobs; a computation there slows them down for everyone, and
many clusters kill it. The compute nodes are reached only through Slurm. They
are grouped into partitions, such as nodes with GPUs or nodes for long jobs,
each with its own limits.

A job asks for resources on a partition and is charged to an account, usually
that of the project. Slurm queues it, and when it can grant the resources on
some nodes, it runs the script of the job there, inside the allocation: the
CPUs, the memory, and the GPUs granted, for the time granted.


## A job gets what it asks for, and no more {#sec-request}

The resources a job asks for are a hard limit. A job that runs past its time is
ended, with the state `TIMEOUT`, and a job that uses more memory than it asked
for is killed, with the state `OUT_OF_MEMORY`, often with no more than a line
about an `oom_kill` in its output. Both lose whatever the job had not yet
written. Asking for too much is no safer: a large request waits longer for
resources to become free, uses up the share of the project, and keeps them
from others. Measure what a job used (@sec-after), and ask for a little more
than that.

Slurm grants CPUs but does not make a program use them. A program uses as many
threads as it is told, or as it decides itself, and many libraries, such as the
linear algebra under NumPy and R, count every core of the node, not those
granted. With too many threads, they compete for the granted CPUs and the
program runs slower than with fewer; with too few, the CPUs idle. Pass the
number granted, `$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK`, to the program and to its libraries,
such as with `OMP_NUM_THREADS` (@sec-script).


## Tasks, CPUs, and nodes {#sec-tasks}

A task is a process. `--ntasks` asks for several processes that work together,
as a program written with MPI does, and `srun` starts the program once per
task. Most research programs are a single process with several threads, which
is one task with several CPUs, `--cpus-per-task`. Asking for `--ntasks=8`
instead gives eight CPUs that may lie on different nodes, which one process
cannot use, and `srun` would start the program eight times.

`--mem` is the memory per node, and `--mem-per-cpu` the memory per CPU. The
script of a job with several nodes runs on the first of them; only `srun`
reaches the others.


## The queue: priority and backfill {#sec-queue}

Slurm starts waiting jobs by their priority, which grows with the time a job
has waited and shrinks with the resources that its account has used recently,
its fair share. While a large job waits for enough nodes to become free,
Slurm fills the gap with smaller jobs, as long as they end before the large job
could start; this backfill is why a job with a short time limit often starts at
once while a long one waits. Ask for an honest time, not the maximum of the
partition. `squeue` shows why a job waits: `Priority` for jobs ahead of it,
`Resources` for resources not yet free, `Dependency` for another job
(@sec-dependencies).


## A job takes the shell along {#sec-environment}

A job runs in the directory it was submitted from, with the environment
variables of the shell that submitted it: the modules loaded, a Python or conda
environment activated, and any variable set by hand travel with the job,
recorded nowhere. The same script, submitted from another shell, computes with
other versions, an undeclared input
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-declared-inputs)). Let the script set up
its environment itself: unload all modules with `module purge`, load those it
needs, and activate its environment (@sec-script).


## Where the files live {#sec-files}

A cluster has several file systems. The home directory is small and backed up,
for code and configuration. A scratch or work file system is large and fast,
for data and results, but not backed up, and many clusters delete files there
that were not used for some weeks. A node-local directory, often `$TMPDIR`, is
the fastest and is deleted when the job ends. The shared file systems are
slow with many small files, as many processes read and write them at once;
pack them, as a Zarr store with shards does
([](../data/zarr.qmd#sec-files)), or copy them to the node-local directory at
the start of the job.


# Working with Slurm {#sec-usage}

A job is a shell script whose first lines, starting with `#SBATCH`, hold the
options of `sbatch`. The same options can be given on the command line of
`sbatch`, where they override those of the script.


## Write a job script {#sec-script}

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=fit-ocean
#SBATCH --partition=cpu
#SBATCH --account=ocean-lab
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out

set -euo pipefail
module purge
module load python/3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

export OMP_NUM_THREADS="$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK"
python fit.py --threads "$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK" --seed 42 --job "$SLURM_JOB_ID"
```

Slurm reads `#SBATCH` lines only up to the first command; one further down is
an ordinary comment, and its option is silently lost. The names of the
partitions, the accounts, and the modules differ from cluster to cluster. Pass
the ID of the job to the program and record it with the results, so that
`sacct` can later tell where and with what a result was computed
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-traceability)). The options used most:

| Option | Asks for |
|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| `--partition`, `--account` | The partition to run on and the account to charge |
| `--cpus-per-task=n` | `n` CPUs for one process (@sec-tasks) |
| `--ntasks=n` | `n` processes, for MPI |
| `--mem=16G`, `--mem-per-cpu=2G` | Memory per node or per CPU; a number without a unit is in megabytes |
| `--time=D-HH:MM:SS` | The time limit; `--time=30` is 30 minutes, and `--time=30:00` as well |
| `--gpus=1` | A GPU; some clusters ask for `--gres=gpu:1` instead |
| `--output=logs/%x-%j.out` | The file for the output, with `%x` for the name of the job and `%j` for its ID |
| `--array`, `--dependency` | Many jobs from one script (@sec-arrays), and jobs that wait for others (@sec-dependencies) |
| `--signal=B:USR1@300` | A signal to the script 300 seconds before the time limit (@sec-checkpoint) |

Without `--output`, the output goes into `slurm-<ID>.out` in the directory the
job was submitted from. Recent versions of Slurm create a missing directory
for the output; on older ones, create it before submitting, or the job fails
without leaving any output.


## Submit, follow, and cancel {#sec-submit}

```bash
sbatch fit.sh                  # prints: Submitted batch job 123456
squeue --me                    # my jobs, and why they wait
squeue --me --start            # when they are expected to start
scontrol show job 123456       # everything about one job
scancel 123456                 # cancel it
```

`sbatch` returns at once; the job runs later, on its own, and the terminal can
be closed. A job that waits shows the reason in the last column of `squeue`
(@sec-queue). `sinfo` lists the partitions and the state of their nodes.


## Work interactively {#sec-interactive}

```bash
srun --cpus-per-task=4 --mem=8G --time=01:00:00 --pty bash
```

An interactive job opens a shell on a compute node, with the resources asked
for, to try a program, debug it, or measure what it needs before writing the
job script. It waits in the queue like any job, and it ends with the shell or
at its time limit. Some clusters offer Jupyter or a desktop through a web
portal, such as Open OnDemand, which starts such a job behind the scenes.


## Many jobs from one script: arrays {#sec-arrays}

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%A_%a.out

config=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" configs.txt)
python fit.py --config "$config" --seed "$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID"
```

An array submits one script as many tasks, each with its own number in
`$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID`, from which it chooses its input, its parameters, or its
seed ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-reproducibility)). `%10` runs at most
ten at once. In `--output`, `%A` is the ID of the array and `%a` the number of
the task. One array is easier on the scheduler than a hundred jobs, and
`scancel` with the ID of the array cancels all of its tasks. The cluster limits
the size of an array, often to about a thousand tasks.


## Jobs that wait for others: dependencies {#sec-dependencies}

```bash
fit=$(sbatch --parsable fit.sh)
sbatch --dependency=afterok:"$fit" plot.sh
```

`afterok` starts the second job only once the first has succeeded, and
`afterany` once it has ended in any way. If the first job fails, a job that
waits with `afterok` stays in the queue for good, with the reason
`DependencyNeverSatisfied`, until it is cancelled. For more than a few steps, a
workflow manager keeps track of what depends on what, and of what is to be
rerun.


## Save a checkpoint before the time limit {#sec-checkpoint}

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --time=24:00:00
#SBATCH --signal=B:USR1@300

trap 'touch stop-and-save' USR1
python simulate.py --resume-from checkpoints/ &
wait    # returns when the signal arrives
wait    # waits until the program has saved and stopped
```

A long computation that saves its state from time to time, a checkpoint, can
continue in a new job where the old one ended, instead of starting over.
`--signal=B:USR1@300` sends the signal `USR1` to the script, `B`, about 300
seconds before the time limit; the script catches it with `trap` and tells the
program to save its state and stop, here with a file the program looks for. The
program runs in the background, with `&`, because the shell handles a signal
only after the command in the foreground has ended. The first `wait` returns
as soon as the signal arrives, and the second waits for the program; without
it, the script, and with it the job, would end before the program has saved.


## Find out what a job used {#sec-after}

```bash
sacct -j 123456 --format=JobID,State,Elapsed,TotalCPU,MaxRSS,ReqMem,ExitCode
seff 123456
```

`sacct` reports on jobs that have ended: their state, such as `COMPLETED`,
`FAILED`, `TIMEOUT`, or `OUT_OF_MEMORY`, how long they ran, the CPU time and
the most memory they used, `MaxRSS`, and their exit code. `seff`, which many
clusters install, sums this up as the share of the CPUs and of the memory
asked for that a job used. A CPU efficiency far below 100 percent means that
the program did not use the CPUs it was granted (@sec-request), and a memory
use far below the request means that the next job can ask for less.
